draft.title: Challenges and Strategies for Offline HTML-to-Markdown Conversion Using Local LLMs and BeautifulSoup
draft.body: A 2025 project shared on r/LocalLLaMA explores converting HTML pages to Markdown offline with local LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B/8B via llama.cpp) running on consumer GPUs. The method first classifies sites as text- or media-focused and uses BeautifulSoup to extract candidate content like titles and headings before the LLM generates extraction strategies and scores output quality. While this approach reportedly yields good results on standard articles, it struggles with media-heavy or JavaScript-rendered content due to lack of browser rendering. Performance per page is reasonable, but batch processing speed might need improvement. Given these constraints, how have others handled dynamic or SPA sites offline? Are there practical ways to enhance static HTML parsing or combine it with local LLMs to better capture asynchronously loaded content without sacrificing offline operation? Insights on balancing extraction accuracy, speed, and complexity would be valuable.

draft.title: Improving Content Extraction for Media-Rich and SPA Websites with Local LLMs: Offline Approaches?
draft.body: The described project uses local LLMs with BeautifulSoup-based HTML analysis to convert web pages to Markdown offline, aiming to outperform classic tools on tricky sites like SPAs or noisy blogs. It detects if a site is text- or media-centric and extracts structural elements before the LLM refines extraction and rates quality. However, without browser rendering, media-heavy and JavaScript-only sites remain challenging. The process runs on GPUs like the 4070 and yields decent per-page speed but may slow with large batches. What are the tradeoffs you've encountered between complexity, speed, and Markdown fidelity?

draft.title: Can local LLMs reliably convert HTML to Markdown offline using BeautifulSoup for content extraction?
draft.body:
A user in a 2025 Reddit thread described a project that uses local LLMs running fully offline to convert HTML pages into high-quality Markdown, aiming to beat traditional tools especially on complex, text-heavy sites. The approach involves first analyzing whether a site is text-focused or media-centric and then using BeautifulSoup to extract key content areas like titles and headings before feeding that to the model.

Given the reliance on static HTML parsing without browser rendering, I wonder how well this method handles modern web apps with dynamic or JavaScript-heavy content. Does the BeautifulSoup-based extraction limit the quality of Markdown output when the actual main content is loaded asynchronously? Has anyone experimented with combining offline LLMs and static HTML parsing to improve Markdown accuracy on such tricky sites?
